name: Fifty Facts About Yourself
description: Generate raw personal material by listing plain facts about yourself without trying to be funny; the funny emerges naturally from honest specifics.
instructions: 1) Write down 50 facts about yourself — just facts, no jokes (e.g. 'I'm the youngest of four', 'I've never had a cavity'). 2) Do about 10 per day so you don't burn out. 3) Do NOT try to be funny; let lines be funny by accident (~1% will be). 4) Review the list and circle facts with tension, embarrassment, or oddity. 5) Pick circled facts and expand each into a premise: why is it weird, what's the problem with it, what does it say about you?
setup: pen and paper or notes app
origin: Common open-mic prep advice; popularized in beginner stand-up curricula (Stand Up Comedy Clinic / Gold Comedy homework)
variations: Variant: 50 opinions instead of facts; or 50 facts about your hometown/family/job.

name: Nine Prompts
description: Fill-in-the-blank prompt sheet that surfaces your natural comedic point of view by forcing honest gut answers, then layering 'because' explanations.
instructions: Round 1: complete these nine prompts with truthful, fast, one-word(ish) answers without overthinking: I hate ___, I love ___, I'm annoyed by ___, The best is when ___, I'm proud that ___, I'm terrified of ___, I'm embarrassed by ___, I'm obsessed with ___, You should totally be my friend because ___. Round 2: add 'because…' to each answer and explain. Extra credit: reverse the categories (what you wrote under love, argue you hate it) and explain. Extra-extra credit: pick one prompt and generate 10+ short answers to build a list joke.
origin: GOLD Comedy workshop homework
variations: Reverse-prompt round; list-joke expansion round.

name: 15-Minute Topic Freewrite
description: Nonstop timed writing on one topic to bypass the inner censor and surface unexpected funny associations.
instructions: 1) Pick a topic or small object (e.g. 'gum', 'being a twin'). 2) Set a timer for 15 minutes. 3) Write everything you can think of about it without stopping and without trying to be funny — memories, opinions, weird facts, complaints. 4) When the timer ends, highlight the ~20% with comedic potential (surprises, strong feelings, odd images). 5) Turn each highlight into a one-line premise to develop later.
origin: Comic Elsa Waithe, via GOLD Comedy; standard freewriting adapted to comedy
variations: Do 5-minute sprints on three topics instead; or freewrite out loud into a voice recorder.

name: Twitter Fitter (Story Compression)
description: Repeatedly rewrite the same anecdote at shrinking word counts to learn economy of language and find the core funny idea.
instructions: 1) Pick a personal anecdote. 2) Write it at full length, about 250 words. 3) Rewrite it in 100 words. 4) Rewrite in 50 words. 5) Rewrite in 25 words. 6) Rewrite in 140 characters. At each stage keep only what's essential to the laugh; notice which details survive — those are the joke.
setup: pen and paper or text editor
origin: Comic Kerri Louise, via GOLD Comedy
variations: Final stage: compress to a single setup/punchline two-liner.

name: News You Can Use (Headline Riffing)
description: Daily drill connecting news headlines to your own life with a fixed formula, building riffing speed and topical-joke muscles.
instructions: 1) Open today's news. 2) Grab a headline. 3) Complete the formula: 'X happened. If that happened to me / in my life…' and write where it goes. 4) Write 10 of these per day without forcing the funny. 5) Keep any that get a smile; the daily reps are the point — your hit rate rises over weeks.
origin: Comic Eddie Sarfaty, via GOLD Comedy; classic late-night monologue training
variations: Late-night style: write 5 setup/punchline monologue jokes per headline instead.

name: But Statements
description: Build joke premises by attaching a realistic problem to an ordinary intention with the word 'but', creating instant comedic tension.
instructions: 1) Write a setup describing an experience, observation, or opinion ('I wanted to impress my date…'). 2) Add 'but'. 3) Finish with a realistic problem ('…but I only know facts about serial killers'). 4) Generate 10 but-statements in 3-5 minutes. 5) Pick the best one and spend 3-5 minutes writing the story/bit it implies, including dialogue and your reactions.
origin: Creative Stand-Up (creativestandup.com) exercise set
variations: Use provided prompts vs. generating your own; escalate by chaining two 'but's.

name: Mismatch Scenarios
description: Generate comedy by putting an incongruous character into a situation (grandma at a rap battle) and writing the believable-but-wrong outcomes.
instructions: 1) Pick or invent a mismatch: cheap person at a fancy restaurant, vegan at a BBQ, grandma at a rap battle. 2) Set a 3-5 minute timer. 3) Write a short story of what happens, aiming for weird or inappropriate yet believable outcomes. 4) Frame it as a hypothetical ('Imagine if…') or as personal narrative ('My grandma once…'). 5) Repeat with 3 different mismatches; keep the funniest beats as bit material.
origin: Creative Stand-Up exercise set; incongruity theory applied
variations: Reverse: normal person in an absurd place.

name: World's Dumbest Museum Tour
description: Mine an absurd real-world subject (an obscure museum) for commentary by imagining being both visitor and tour guide.
instructions: 1) Search online for obscure real museums (Toilet Museum, Barbed Wire Museum, SPAM Museum). 2) Pick one. 3) Write/riff as a patron: what do you see, what's the gift shop, who else is here? 4) Then riff as the tour guide: deliver a deadpan guided tour aloud, committing fully. 5) Record yourself; keep the lines that land.
origin: Creative Stand-Up exercise set
variations: Swap museum for any weird real product page or local attraction.

name: "Hey, That's Not Right" Comedy Journal
description: A 7-day observational journal logging things that feel off or absurd in daily life, then drafting playful responses to each.
instructions: 1) Each day for 7 days, write 5-10 things you noticed that felt off, weird, wrong, or inappropriate. 2) For each item, ask: how would my favorite comedian frame this? 3) Write a 'playfully inappropriate' response or one-liner for each. 4) At week's end, review the log and pull the 3 strongest premises into longer bits.
origin: Creative Stand-Up exercise set; classic observational-comedy journaling
variations: Theme days: only things at work, only things on your commute.

name: Random Sentence Joke Diagnosis
description: Use randomly generated sentences as raw setups, interrogating each with three structural questions to train joke-mechanics instincts.
instructions: 1) Use an online random sentence generator to produce 10 sentences. 2) For each, ask: (a) Can I shatter an assumption the sentence creates? (b) Is there a double meaning / alternate interpretation of a word? (c) Are dissimilar ideas present that I can juxtapose? 3) Draft at least one joke per sentence using whichever question fired. 4) Refine the best ones by adding character, setting, or conflict.
origin: Jerry Corley, Stand Up Comedy Clinic
variations: Use random Wikipedia article titles or fortune-cookie slips instead.

name: Inflection Angle-Finding
description: Repeat one sentence aloud emphasizing a different word each time; each emphasis implies a different scene and comedic angle.
instructions: 1) Pick a simple sentence ('I never said she stole my money'). 2) Say it aloud, stressing word 1; note what scenario that emphasis implies. 3) Repeat for each word in the sentence. 4) For each implied scenario, write a quick comedic response or tag. 5) Notice how many distinct jokes one line yields purely from delivery.
origin: Jerry Corley, Stand Up Comedy Clinic
variations: Do it with one of your existing punchlines to find the optimal stress word.

name: Joke Mine (Greg Dean Joke Prospector)
description: Greg Dean's systematic method for engineering punchlines: list a setup's assumptions, find the connector, reinterpret it, and write the punch from the second story.
instructions: 1) Write or pick a setup (a neutral statement about a topic). 2) List the assumptions an audience makes hearing it (the '1st story'). 3) Pick one target assumption to shatter. 4) Identify the connector — the word/phrase in the setup that supports that assumption. 5) List reinterpretations of the connector (other meanings/contexts). 6) Choose one reinterpretation and imagine the '2nd story' it implies. 7) Write a punchline that reveals the 2nd story. 8) Repeat with other assumptions to mine multiple punchlines per setup.
setup: Greg Dean's worksheet format helpful but optional
origin: Greg Dean, Step by Step to Stand-Up Comedy
variations: Joke Map variant: start from a topic, generate setups first, then mine each.

name: Punchline-First Fishbowl
description: Keep a jar/file of orphan punchlines and funny lines, and regularly draw one at random to write a whole bit backwards from it.
instructions: 1) Maintain a fishbowl (or note file) where you drop every stray funny line, tagline, or punchline you think of. 2) Daily or weekly, draw one at random. 3) Ask: what setup would make this line a surprise? What story ends here? 4) Write the bit backwards: premise, setup, then the drawn line as the punch. 5) Return lines that didn't work — they may pay off later.
setup: jar + slips of paper, or a notes file
origin: Attributed to Dave Chappelle's practice; reported in comedy-writing blogs
variations: Pair variant: swap fishbowls with another comic and write setups for each other's punchlines.

name: This-Is-Like-That Comparison Reps
description: Daily reps writing 'X is like Y' comparisons to train the analogy reflex underlying a huge share of jokes.
instructions: 1) Pick 5 everyday things (your commute, group chats, a food). 2) For each, write 5 completions of 'X is like Y' reaching into unrelated domains ('Group texts are like jury duty: mandatory, endless, and someone always talks too much'). 3) Push past obvious comparisons — the 4th and 5th are usually the funny ones. 4) Add a 'because' clause that sharpens the link. 5) Do daily; speed and oddness improve with reps.
origin: Common comedy-writing practice; described by working comics in writing-practice articles
variations: Constraint version: comparisons must come from a random category (sports, history, food).

name: Toplyn Monologue Joke Method
description: Joe Toplyn's late-night system practiced as a drill: turn a headline into a joke via handles, associations, and one of six Punch Line Makers.
instructions: 1) Pick a news headline that triggers a reaction ('that's weird'). 2) Identify 1-2 'handles' — the elements with well-known associations (e.g. 'snail', 'Los Angeles'). 3) Brainstorm associations for each handle (snail: slow, slimy, eaten by the French). 4) Generate a punchline with a Punch Line Maker: link two associations; link the topic to pop culture; ask a question about the topic and answer with an unexpected association; find a play on words; visualize the topic; or imagine related sub-topics. 5) Write a rough draft joining topic and punch with an 'angle' (transition logic). 6) Rewrite: add believable specifics, cut distracting words, end on the funniest word ('backload'). Do 5 headlines per session.
origin: Joe Toplyn, Comedy Writing for Late-Night TV
variations: Pick one Punch Line Maker and force 10 jokes using only that tool.

name: Roast Joke Construction Drill
description: Systematically write roast jokes about a person (with consent, or a celebrity) by brainstorming their associations and linking them in surprising ways.
instructions: 1) Pick a target: a consenting friend or a celebrity. 2) List 15+ associations — things an audience would accept as true (deeds, looks, family, scandals); emphasize unflattering ones. 3) Write jokes by: linking two associations together; asking a question about them and answering with an unexpected association; finding wordplay in their name/details. 4) Edit to avoid the on-the-nose direct insult — go indirect (instead of 'you look like a scarecrow': 'who's been scaring crows off our crops?'). 5) Cut to your 5 best, varying which trait each targets. 6) Read them aloud for rhythm.
origin: Joe Toplyn (How to Write a Roast); Comedy Central roast tradition
variations: Self-roast version: write 5 roast jokes about yourself — great for self-deprecating openers.

name: Roast Battle Fact Exchange
description: Pair exercise modeled on roast battles: partners exchange 10 true facts about themselves, then each writes 5 roast jokes from the other's facts.
instructions: 1) Pair with a willing partner (comic friend). 2) Exchange lists of 10 true facts about yourselves that could be joke ammunition (job, habits, appearance, history). 3) Separately, each writes at least 15 roast jokes from the other's facts, then cuts to the best 5. 4) Meet and take turns delivering jokes battle-style, alternating. 5) Debrief: which jokes landed, which felt mean without funny. 6) Rewrite the misses.
setup: a consenting partner; a week lead time
origin: Roast battle scene (Comedy Store Roast Battle format), described by working comics
variations: Speed version: 24-hour turnaround; or both roast the same third-party celebrity and compare.

name: Commercial Parody One-Change
description: Write a parody of a specific commercial changing exactly one element, training the 'game' instinct — one clear comedic deviation, everything else played straight.
instructions: 1) Pick a real, specific commercial (or genre of commercial) you know well. 2) Identify its conventions: tone, structure, visuals, voice-over style. 3) Change exactly ONE element (the product is absurd, the spokesperson is wrong, one assumption is false). 4) Write the parody keeping everything else faithfully identical, under 2.5 pages. 5) Read aloud; check the single game is clear and heightens 3+ times.
origin: UCB Sketch 101 assignment
variations: Genre parody version: alter one convention of a film/TV genre instead.

name: Logical Response Reversal
description: Vorhaus drill: for any situation, identify the expected response, then write its opposite or a wildly inappropriate alternative.
instructions: 1) Pick a mundane situation (boss asks you to stay late; waiter recites specials). 2) Write the logical, expected response. 3) Now write the opposite response, and 2-3 wildly inappropriate-but-internally-logical responses. 4) Pick the funniest and write a beat of dialogue where a character commits to it completely. 5) Repeat for 5 situations per session.
origin: John Vorhaus, The Comic Toolbox
variations: Do it live in improv: partner feeds situations, you answer with the inappropriate response in character.

name: Clash of Context Generator
description: Generate comic premises by forcing the union of incompatible elements — a gap between comic reality and real reality.
instructions: 1) Make two columns: column A = ordinary settings/roles (funeral, IT helpdesk, kindergarten); column B = incompatible worlds/attitudes (heavy metal, medieval knight, cult leader). 2) Randomly pair one from each. 3) For each pairing write the premise sentence: 'What if X operated in Y?' 4) List 5 specific comic moments the clash produces. 5) Keep pairings that generate moments effortlessly — that's a real premise. Do 5-10 pairings per session, expecting 9 of 10 to fail (Rule of Nine).
origin: John Vorhaus, The Comic Toolbox (comic premise; clash of context)
variations: Use a random noun generator for column entries.

name: Pause Placement Drill
description: Deliberately practice where and how long to pause in a joke, testing the same line with different timing on different listeners.
instructions: 1) Take one of your jokes (or a stock joke). 2) Record yourself delivering it three ways: no pause; short beat before the punchline; long 'pregnant pause' before the punchline. 3) Listen back and mark which version creates the most anticipation. 4) Try the best version on 2-3 different people on different days and compare reactions. 5) Repeat with the pause AFTER the punchline (riding the laugh) — count two beats before continuing.
origin: Standard stand-up/acting pedagogy; MasterClass and acting-school timing guides
variations: Pacing version: deliver the same joke fast, medium, slow and compare.

name: Same Joke, Different Rooms
description: Field-test one joke on several different people/groups, varying only timing and emphasis, to learn that timing is an interaction with listeners.
instructions: 1) Pick one joke or funny story you like. 2) Over a week, tell it to at least 5 different people or small groups in natural conversation. 3) Each time vary one variable: pause length, speed, which word you stress, or deadpan vs. animated face. 4) Immediately after, jot what you changed and how big the laugh was. 5) Converge on the optimal delivery; notice it may differ by audience.
origin: Steve Martin's dictum that timing is an interaction with the audience; common comedy-class fieldwork
variations: Tell the same story at three different social events and track which beats always work.

name: Stranger Conversation Reps (Crowd Work Gym)
description: Practice the crowd-work loop — listen, diagnose, respond playfully — in everyday conversations with strangers, off stage.
instructions: 1) In daily life (cafés, lines, Ubers) start small conversations with strangers. 2) Run the crowd-work loop: ask a simple question (name, work, where from); listen for the first unusual detail; repeat their answer back in your own words; then 'agree and heighten' — treat their odd detail as gospel and twist it one notch absurd. 3) Aim for play, not jokes; the goal is reps in listening-then-responding. 4) Afterward note any line that got a laugh; these become crowd-work openers. Do 1-3 conversations daily.
origin: Common advice from working comics (Hot Breath VIP, School of Laughs, funnymuscle.com)
variations: Socratic version: only ask questions and mirror; no jokes allowed for a week, then add punches.

name: Crowd Work Game Film Review
description: Record every set or social riff session and review it like game film, logging improvised lines that worked.
instructions: 1) Record every open mic/set (audio is enough), or record yourself riffing with friends. 2) Within 24 hours, listen back. 3) Log: improvised lines that got laughs ('gems'), moments you talked over a laugh, dead pauses, and crutch words. 4) Transfer gems into your material file; script the best improvised crowd-work lines as reusable openers. 5) Pick ONE delivery fix to focus on next set.
origin: Universal stand-up practice; emphasized by funnymuscle.com and open-mic coaching
variations: Video version adds body-language review.

name: One Funny Line a Day Challenge
description: 30-day field exercise: deliberately attempt one funny line (sarcasm, exaggeration, playful tease) in a real conversation every day.
instructions: 1) Each day for 30 days, attempt at least one intentionally funny line in a live conversation, in your natural humor style. 2) Keep stakes low: aim for a smile, not a roar. 3) Log each attempt at night: what you said, context, reaction. 4) Weekly, review the log for patterns — which styles (self-deprecation, exaggeration, absurd agreement) land for you. 5) Double down on your top style in week 4.
origin: Self-improvement comedy guides (Inner Mastery Hub; Big Belly Comedy Club)
variations: Pair version: a friend does it too; trade logs and feedback weekly.

name: Pun Sprint
description: Timed wordplay drill: pick a topic and generate as many puns on it as possible, exploiting homophones, double meanings, and twisted clichés.
instructions: 1) Pick a topic noun (cheese, dentists, camping). 2) Set 5 minutes. 3) List topic-related words, then for each find: homophones/sound-alikes, second meanings, idioms/clichés containing them. 4) Force at least 10 puns by swapping the topic word into clichés ('No whey!'). 5) Read the list aloud to a friend and keep the 2 that get groans-with-smiles. Play as a pair game by alternating puns until someone dries up.
origin: Pun communities / O. Henry Pun-Off style warmups; Mel Helitzer's POW (Play On Words) chapter formalizes it
variations: Pun-Off duel: two players alternate puns on one topic, 5-second shot clock.

name: Cliché Twisting (Helitzer POW Drill)
description: Take familiar clichés and idioms and twist them — substitute, extend, or literalize — since over half of humor rides on reshaped familiar phrases.
instructions: 1) Collect 10 clichés/idioms ('money can't buy happiness', 'early bird gets the worm'). 2) For each, try three twists: (a) substitution — swap one word for a sound-alike or topic word; (b) extension — agree then add a turn ('...but it can rent it'); (c) literalization — treat the metaphor as physically true and describe the consequences. 3) Write at least one twisted version per cliché. 4) Save winners as one-liners. Repeat weekly with fresh clichés.
origin: Mel Helitzer & Mark Shatz, Comedy Writing Secrets (POW chapter)
variations: Do it with proverbs from other cultures, or with corporate jargon.

name: Tag Your Best Laughs
description: Scotty Meltzer's homework: take your jokes that already work and systematically write tags — extra punchlines after the punchline — using a menu of tagging methods.
instructions: 1) List your 5 best-performing jokes. 2) For each, write tags using each method: (a) POV shift — react as another character/object in the joke; (b) example tag — make the subtext explicit or give 2-3 concrete instances; (c) new shatter — break a different assumption in the same setup; (d) reaction tag — comment on your own joke or the audience's reaction; (e) denial capper — apologize for/deny the joke, then punch again ('Just kidding... my mother thinks you're boring too'); (f) physical tag — mime the consequence silently. 3) Aim for 5-10 tags per joke. 4) Test live; keep tags until one stops the laugh roll.
origin: Scotty Meltzer, 'Be Funnier' column (IJA); standard stand-up craft
variations: Group punch-up version: friends pitch tags for your punchline, 10 alts minimum.

name: Plant and Harvest (Callback Drill)
description: Deliberately plant a line early in a set or conversation, then 'harvest' it later in an unexpected context to create callback laughs.
instructions: 1) In your current 5-minute set (or a dinner-party story), choose one distinctive line or image from an early joke — it need not be a punchline. 2) Write 3 later moments where it could return in a new context. 3) Script the best one as a callback. 4) Perform and note the reaction — callbacks typically get cheers, not just laughs. 5) Practice in conversation too: reference something said 20 minutes earlier, twisted to fit the new moment.
setup: an existing set or planned conversation
origin: Stand-up craft; articulated by Scotty Meltzer and improv reincorporation (Johnstone)
variations: Conversation version: call back a friend's line from earlier in the evening.

name: The Follow Game
description: At an open mic, write material in real time off every performer's set as if you were going up next, training riffing and association under mild pressure.
instructions: 1) Attend an open mic with a notebook; sit where you can write. 2) For every performer, write what their material makes you think of: a tag for their joke, a related premise from your life, an opposite take. 3) Pretend you're up next and must reference the show so far. 4) Leave with 10+ raw ideas. 5) Next day, develop the best 2 into bits.
origin: Bjorn RG, 'The Joke Exploder' blog
variations: TV version: do it watching a late-night monologue, pausing after each joke to write your own tag.

name: The "I'm Like" Game
description: Rapid metaphor game: justify why you are 'like' any random noun, saying the first connection that comes to mind.
instructions: 1) Solo: open a random-noun generator. Pair: partner calls out nouns. 2) For each noun, complete aloud: 'I'm like [noun] because [reason]' — first thought, no overthinking ('I'm like a shopping cart: one bad wheel and full of stuff nobody needs'). 3) Do 10-20 nouns per session. 4) Note the comparisons that surprised you; expand winners into self-deprecating bits.
origin: Bjorn RG, 'The Joke Exploder' blog
variations: Third-person version: 'My boss is like…', 'Dating apps are like…'.

name: Total Opposites
description: Take any opinion or idea and argue its exact opposite to find fresh angles and break habitual takes.
instructions: 1) Write 5 opinions you actually hold ('brunch is great'). 2) For each, write the opposite stance and spend 3 minutes earnestly arguing it with specifics ('brunch is a scam: $19 eggs and day-drinking with extra steps'). 3) Notice the opposite take is often the fresher comedic angle. 4) Also apply to performance habits: if you always talk fast, do a set slow; if you never swear, write clean, etc.
origin: Bjorn RG, 'The Joke Exploder' blog; echoes Vorhaus's opposite tool
variations: Debate version: friend defends the normal take, you must win with the absurd one.

name: Play Tag (Premise → Punchline Volume Drill)
description: Volume drill: write as many punchlines as possible for one premise, then twist the premise and write more, then quality-check against a checklist.
instructions: 1) Pick a premise ('self-checkout machines treat you like a criminal'). 2) Write punchlines until dry — aim 10+. 3) Find a twist on the premise (POV of the machine; year 2050 version) and write 5+ more. 4) Repeat with a second twist. 5) Audit every punchline: keep those with at least 2 of — surprise, wordplay/pun, rhyme/alliteration, clever observation, reference to a known phrase. 6) Best 2-3 go in your set.
origin: Bjorn RG, 'The Joke Exploder' blog; mirrors writers-room alts culture
variations: Group version: everyone pitches punchlines on a shared premise, building on each other (New Girl room style).

name: Ten Alts (Writers' Room Alternatives)
description: For any existing joke line, generate ten alternative punchlines — the standard sitcom-room discipline that stretches you past your first idea.
instructions: 1) Take a line that's supposed to be funny (yours, or from a script/sitcom with sound muted at the punchline). 2) Write 10 alternative punchlines for the same setup. Number them; do not stop at 3 good ones — the surprise often arrives at #7-10. 3) If in a group, go around the room pitching alts and building on each other's. 4) Compare your best alt to the original; analyze why the winner wins.
setup: a script, sitcom scene, or your own jokes
origin: TV writers' room practice; described by New Girl showrunner Liz Meriwether
variations: Mute-the-punchline version: pause a sitcom before each punchline and pitch your own, then compare.

name: Gag Pass on a Script
description: Do a systematic comedy pass over any piece of writing (yours or a friend's), inserting at least one joke per page across a checklist of humor categories.
instructions: 1) Take a finished piece (story, speech, sketch, essay). 2) Sweep it category by category looking for joke opportunities: funny names; funnier settings; visual/sound gags; physical comedy; reveals and surprises; references; character reactions; background gags; wordplay; callbacks/running jokes. 3) Enforce density: at least one laugh per page or scene. 4) End every scene/section with a 'button' (closing joke). 5) Build one extended comic set piece. 6) Read aloud and cut jokes that break the piece's internal logic.
origin: TV/film punch-up practice; Shaula Evans method (The Black List forums)
variations: Swap drafts with a friend and punch up each other's pages.

name: Generate 100 Topics
description: Rapid-fire brainstorm of 100 potential comedy topics from prompt categories, building a material bank you mine for months.
instructions: 1) Set up prompt categories: foods, fears, celebrities, family members, jobs you've had, things you've quit, places, pet peeves, firsts, possessions. 2) List items rapidly under each until you total 100. No judging, no jokes yet. 3) Star the 10 with emotional charge. 4) Keep the list; whenever you need material, pull a starred topic and run a freewrite or joke-structure drill on it.
origin: New Zealand Comedy School writing workbook; common comedy-class first assignment
variations: Do 100 'things that annoy me' for a rant-comedy bank.

name: Two-Minute Topic Sprints
description: Pull random nouns from a bag and freewrite two minutes on each — high-rep angle-finding under time pressure.
instructions: 1) Write 20 random nouns on slips; put in a bag (or use a generator). 2) Draw one. 3) Freewrite for exactly 2 minutes: opinions, memories, weird facts, questions. 4) Draw the next; do 5-10 per session. 5) Afterwards underline anything with an attitude (love/hate/fear/confusion) — those become premises. The time cap forces instinct over polish.
origin: New Zealand Comedy School writing workbook
variations: Spoken version: riff aloud into a recorder instead of writing.

name: Deep Topic Mining
description: Exhaust a single topic across 3-5 pages of lists, mind-maps, facts, associations, questions, and wordplay before writing any jokes.
instructions: 1) Choose one starred topic (e.g. 'weddings'). 2) Produce 3-5 pages: a fact list; an association mind-map; a list of every cliché and stock phrase about it; questions you have about it; wordplay on its key terms; your personal history with it; what makes you angry/scared/confused about it. 3) Only then write jokes, using the richest veins. 4) Note how punchlines come easier with the excavation done.
origin: New Zealand Comedy School writing workbook; mirrors Toplyn's association maps
variations: Group mining: each person takes a branch of the mind-map.

name: Emotional Tagging Pass
description: Review your raw notes and label every idea with the emotion it carries — comedy lives where feeling is strongest.
instructions: 1) Take a week of raw notes/freewrites. 2) Label each idea with an emotion tag: fear, anger, joy, shame, confusion, disgust, love. 3) For the strongest tags, write what exactly causes the emotion ('it's not the wedding, it's the group dance instructions'). 4) Convert the top 5 into premise sentences that keep the emotion explicit ('It's infuriating that...'). 5) These become setups delivered WITH that attitude.
origin: New Zealand Comedy School workbook; Judy Carter's attitude pedagogy
variations: Carter's four-question version below (Weird/Hard/Scary/Stupid).

name: Weird-Hard-Scary-Stupid Premise Drill
description: Judy Carter's core drill: pick a topic and answer 'What's weird / hard / scary / stupid about it?', then rant the answer aloud holding one attitude.
instructions: 1) Pick a topic from your life (commuting, group chats, your gym). 2) Write four sentences: 'What's WEIRD about X is...', 'What's HARD about X is...', 'What's SCARY about X is...', 'What's STUPID about X is...'. Be logical and truthful, not jokey. 3) Choose the sentence with the most heat. 4) Rant on it aloud for 60-90 seconds, emphasizing every word with the chosen emotion, adding specifics as they come. 5) Record; transcribe the funny accidents; structure them into setup → punchline → act-out.
origin: Judy Carter, The Comedy Bible / Stand-Up Comedy: The Book
variations: Partner version: partner picks your topic and the attitude; you must rant on demand.

name: Joke Autopsy
description: Transcribe a great comedian's joke verbatim and dissect why it works — setup, assumptions, punch word placement, rhythm — then write one in the same skeleton.
instructions: 1) Pick a joke that kills (from a special). 2) Transcribe it word for word. 3) Mark: the setup's planted assumption; the connector word; the punch word and its position (usually last); pause placement; act-outs. 4) Write WHY the laugh happens in one sentence. 5) Now write your own joke on a different topic using the identical skeleton. 6) Repeat weekly with different comics to absorb varied structures.
origin: New Zealand Comedy School workbook; universal comedy-class assignment
variations: Autopsy a joke that BOMBED and diagnose the failure.

name: Ten Jokes by Formula
description: Momentum drill: write 10 complete setup/punchline jokes in one sitting using known formulas, accepting that most will be bad (Rule of Nine).
instructions: 1) Choose 2-3 formulas: rule of three (two straight, one absurd); comparison ('X is like Y'); misdirection (setup implies A, punch reveals B); literalization of an idiom. 2) Using your topic bank, write 10 complete jokes — finished sentences, not fragments. 3) Don't edit mid-flow. 4) Next day, pick the best 2 and rewrite each 3 ways. 5) Track your weekly joke count; volume is the metric, not quality.
origin: New Zealand Comedy School workbook; standard course homework
variations: Constraint: all 10 jokes on ONE topic; or all 10 using ONE formula.

name: Joke Tightening Pass
description: Editing drill: take 10 old jokes and cut excess words, clarify setups, backload punch words, and sharpen attitude.
instructions: 1) Pull 10 jokes from your notebook (including duds). 2) For each: cut every word not needed for the laugh; move the funniest word to the end; replace generic nouns with specific ones (not 'a car' — 'a 2009 Camry'); make the setup one breath long; check the attitude is consistent. 3) Read before/after versions aloud; the after should land harder and faster. 4) Keep a 'cuts I always need' list to internalize your habits.
origin: New Zealand Comedy School workbook; standard punch-up craft
variations: Trade jokes with a friend and tighten each other's.

name: Fix a Bombed Joke
description: Take a weak joke you saw bomb (at a mic or online) and rewrite it until it works — practice only, never perform someone else's premise.
instructions: 1) At an open mic or in a YouTube comment-section clip, find a joke that didn't land. 2) Write it down. 3) Diagnose: unclear setup? telegraphed punch? no attitude? wrong punch word position? 4) Rewrite it 3 ways fixing different diagnoses. 5) Compare with the original to articulate the lesson. 6) File under 'craft practice' — never perform it; the exercise is diagnostic skill.
setup: open mic or clips to study
origin: New Zealand Comedy School workbook
variations: Fix one of YOUR bombed jokes 24 hours after the mic, while the memory is fresh.

name: Rule of Three Reps
description: Drill the most reliable joke pattern: two expected items establish a pattern, the third breaks it.
instructions: 1) Write 10 list setups: 'My three favorite things about X are...', 'X requires three skills...'. 2) For each, write two genuine, pattern-establishing items, then brainstorm 5 candidate third items that break the pattern (absurd, dark, petty, too-honest). 3) Pick the third item that's surprising AND inevitable in hindsight. 4) Read aloud — the rhythm should be da-da-DUM. 5) Sprinkle your best triples into conversation this week and note reactions.
origin: Classical comic structure; taught in Comedy Bible, Comedy Writing Secrets, speechwriting courses
variations: Speech version: build a triple into a toast or presentation opener.

name: Top Ten List Writing
description: Write a Letterman-style Top Ten list on a topic, forcing many distinct angles on a single premise.
instructions: 1) Pick a list title with built-in tension ('Top Ten Signs Your Roommate Is a Cult Leader'). 2) Brainstorm 20+ entries — each must attack the premise from a different angle (visual, wordplay, escalation, hyper-specific, meta). 3) Cut to the 10 best, ordered so the strongest are #10 (opens), #5, #2-1 (closers). 4) Read aloud for rhythm; entries should be one breath each. 5) Weekly habit: one list per week builds angle variety fast.
origin: Late Night with David Letterman tradition; Judy Carter exercise lists
variations: Group version: writers-room pitch — everyone shouts entries, scribe captures, vote the ten.

name: Emotional Rollercoaster Act-Out
description: Deliver the same act-out line through different emotional filters (anger, fear, disgust...) and compare recordings to find the funniest emotional truth.
instructions: 1) Pick a line from your set, ideally an act-out (first-person dialogue). 2) Record yourself delivering it 7 times, each with a different emotion: anger, sadness, happiness, fear, confusion, surprise, disgust. 3) Play back and note how the emotion changes the laugh potential. 4) Pick the strongest filter and re-record twice more, committing harder. 5) Update your set notes with the chosen emotional read.
origin: Acting-for-comics training (English Comedy Frankfurt workshop)
variations: Do it with a neutral sentence ('the bus was late') to isolate pure emotional coloring.

name: Listen and React (Imaginary Partner)
description: Perform a joke while imagining a scene partner or audience member responding, and practice visibly reacting — trains presence and act-out realism.
instructions: 1) Choose a joke involving another person (real or implied). 2) Perform it on camera, imagining that person present; pause where they would speak. 3) React authentically in different ways across takes: surprise, agreement, offense, rebuttal. 4) Watch back: do your reactions read as real listening? 5) On stage, apply the same skill to actual audience reactions — acknowledge, react, continue.
origin: Acting-for-comics training (English Comedy Frankfurt workshop)
variations: Pair version: friend plays the scene partner improvising responses.

name: Gesture Amplification Pass
description: Go through a set adding deliberate, exaggerated physical choices to punchlines, then dial back to what serves each joke.
instructions: 1) Video yourself doing 3 minutes of material standing still. 2) Do a second take where every joke gets an exaggerated physical choice: posture shift, hand motion, facial take, frozen pose. 3) Compare takes; mark jokes that gained from physicality. 4) Third take: keep only the gestures that helped, at 70% intensity. 5) Note where stillness IS the joke (deadpan).
origin: Acting-for-comics training (English Comedy Frankfurt workshop)
variations: Silent-movie version: perform the bit with gestures only, no words, then restore words.

name: Mirror-Then-Record Set Rehearsal
description: Structured rehearsal ladder before an open mic: out loud, then mirror, then audio, then video, fixing one layer at a time.
instructions: 1) Once you have ~5 minutes of material, say it out loud (not in your head) — new ideas will appear; capture them. 2) Run it in front of a mirror to find physical gags and check expressions. 3) Audio-record a run; listen for flow, pauses, timing, filler words. 4) Video-record; review body language, mic handling, presence. 5) Rehearse until natural, not memorized-sounding — aim to know the BEATS, not the exact words. 6) Warm up out loud before the mic itself.
origin: Standard open-mic preparation; MasterClass and comedy-club guides
variations: Bullet-point method: rehearse from a 5-word-per-bit setlist instead of a script.

name: Ride-Home Review
description: Listen to your recorded set immediately after the open mic (on the ride home) and log what worked while the context is fresh.
instructions: 1) Record every set. 2) On the way home, listen once through. 3) Note: laughs you didn't expect, silence you didn't expect, lines you flubbed, improvised moments worth keeping. 4) Within 24 hours, update your master document: mark each joke kill/okay/bomb. 5) After 3 mics, drop or rewrite anything that bombed twice.
origin: Open-mic culture standard practice (Comedians on the Loose; club guides)
variations: Spreadsheet version: track each joke's laugh score across mics.

name: Caption Contest Reps
description: Weekly drill writing many captions for a captionless cartoon, then submitting one — trains visual-verbal joke bridging and word economy.
instructions: 1) Each week, open the current New Yorker caption contest cartoon (or any captionless cartoon). 2) Identify the 'handles': the 1-2 most distinctive people/things and their action. 3) Accept the absurd premise fully; write captions that make sense INSIDE it. 4) Write 10+ captions: try linking the two handles, giving the mundane character's POV on the absurd thing, or an idiom twisted by the scene. 5) Cut every unneeded word. 6) Pick your best, submit, and compare with the eventual finalists to calibrate.
origin: New Yorker Cartoon Caption Contest; method articulated by Joe Toplyn and Lawrence Wood
variations: Group version: everyone writes 5 captions for the same cartoon, blind-vote the winner.

name: Humorous Story File + Speech
aliases: Toastmasters 'Know Your Sense of Humor' Project
description: Build a running collection of humorous personal anecdotes, then deliver a short speech built around at least one of them.
instructions: 1) Start a 'humor file': log every story that gets a laugh when you tell it, plus funny things you witness. 2) Weekly, add 2-3 entries with the laugh line marked. 3) Pick one story; structure it for a 5-7 minute speech: setup context, escalating beats, punchline, callback close. 4) Deliver to a group (club, friends, camera). 5) Note where laughs came and re-edit the file entry.
origin: Toastmasters Pathways 'Engaging Humor' path, Level 1
variations: Eulogy/toast version: build the story into a wedding or birthday toast.

name: Impromptu Humor Speech Drill
description: Practice inserting pre-rehearsed funny stories into surprise speech topics, the Toastmasters method for humor under impromptu conditions.
instructions: 1) Prepare 3-5 well-rehearsed short funny stories from your humor file. 2) Have someone give you a random topic (or draw from slips). 3) Speak for 2 minutes on the topic, finding a bridge to one of your stories and adapting its details to fit. 4) Land the story's laugh line, then tie back to the topic. 5) Repeat with new topics until any story can serve any topic.
origin: Toastmasters Engaging Humor path ('Engage Your Audience with Humor' project)
variations: Harder: bridge the SAME story to five different random topics in a row.

name: Analogy from a Single Subject
description: Jerry Corley's strategy: take one subject and force an analogy to something unrelated, mining the surprising differences for punchlines.
instructions: 1) Pick a subject (flight attendant). 2) Choose something it superficially resembles (waitress). 3) List the surprising DIFFERENCES ('a waitress can't kick you out at 30,000 feet'). 4) Write a setup asserting the similarity, then punchlines exposing the differences. 5) Add a physical act-out of the contrast. 6) Repeat with two more analogy targets for the same subject.
origin: Jerry Corley, Stand Up Comedy Clinic ('911 for your Jokes')
variations: Reverse: list surprising SIMILARITIES between truly unlike things.

name: Descriptor + Subject Character Builder
description: Attach a flawed adjective to a role (the passive-aggressive flight attendant) and generate scenarios of that trait in action.
instructions: 1) Take a subject/role. 2) Attach a descriptor that's also a human flaw: lazy, procrastinating, selfish, passive-aggressive, paranoid. 3) Ask: how does this trait show up in their duties? Write 5+ concrete scenarios ('the lazy flight attendant does the safety demo from a seated position'). 4) Perform the strongest as an act-out, in character. 5) Stack scenarios into a bit or Top 10 list.
origin: Jerry Corley, Stand Up Comedy Clinic
variations: Use your own dominant flaw as the descriptor on every job you've had.

name: Fact-Mining a Subject
description: Research real facts, rules, and statistics about a subject and extend them logically to absurd implications.
instructions: 1) Pick a subject. 2) Research 10-15 real facts: quirks, regulations, statistics, history. 3) Flag the ones that seem absurd or contradictory on their face. 4) Apply 'logical extension': if this rule/stat is true, what ridiculous consequence follows? 5) Write observations exposing the built-in absurdity ('The FAA requires X... which means legally, Y'). 6) Cite the real fact in the setup — truth makes the punch hit harder.
origin: Jerry Corley, Stand Up Comedy Clinic
variations: Use your own industry's rules and jargon — insider absurdity is gold.

name: What If Escalation
description: Push a topic through escalating hypotheticals — different contexts, different people, then extreme and more-extreme versions.
instructions: 1) Take a topic. 2) Write 5 'what if' transplants: what if this existed in the 1800s / at a funeral / run by toddlers? 3) Pick the funniest and escalate: write the extreme version, then ask 'and what's MORE extreme?' at least 3 times. 4) Stop one step before it breaks believability — that's usually the act-out. 5) Script the ladder as a bit that heightens beat by beat.
origin: Neil Thornton / NZ Comedy School workbook; mirrors improv heightening
variations: Pair version: alternate escalations until someone breaks.

name: Explore the People (Character Study)
description: Develop the people attached to a topic — speech patterns, shopping lists, hopes and dreams — to unlock character-based material.
instructions: 1) For your topic, list the characters around it (for 'gyms': the trainer, the grunter, the mirror guy). 2) Pick one and build a sheet: how they talk (catchphrases), what's in their shopping cart, their dating profile, their secret fear, their dream. 3) Write a 30-second monologue in their voice and perform it on camera. 4) Extract the lines that pop into act-outs for your set.
origin: Neil Thornton workbook; standard sketch/stand-up character work
variations: Do the sheet for YOURSELF as others see you — instant self-deprecation material.

name: Find Your POV Thesis
description: Force yourself to state, in one sentence, what you're trying to prove about a topic — the spine that turns scattered jokes into a bit.
instructions: 1) Take a topic you have 5+ scattered jokes about. 2) Write one sentence: 'I'm trying to prove that ___' ('weddings are hostage situations with cake'). 3) Audit each joke: does it serve the thesis? Cut or rewrite strays. 4) Re-order surviving jokes so each escalates the case. 5) Write a closer that states the thesis at its most extreme.
origin: Neil Thornton workbook; common comedy-class concept (angle/thesis)
variations: Debate version: defend the thesis aloud against a friend's objections, in persona.

name: Seinfeld Chain (Daily Writing Streak)
description: Productivity ritual attributed to Jerry Seinfeld: write jokes every single day and mark an X on a calendar; the only rule is don't break the chain.
instructions: 1) Put a year calendar on your wall. 2) Define the minimum daily unit: e.g. 15 minutes of joke writing or 3 attempted jokes. 3) Every day you do it, mark a big X. 4) Your only job is to not break the chain — quality is irrelevant on bad days. 5) Review weekly for keepers. The compounding volume is what raises the hit rate.
origin: Attributed to Jerry Seinfeld (via Brad Isaac's Lifehacker story); cited in comedy-writing pedagogy
variations: Tweet-chain version: post one joke per day publicly for accountability.

name: If-Then Heightening Pass
description: UCB sketch/improv drill: once you find the one unusual thing in a premise, repeatedly ask 'if this is true, what else is true?' to generate escalating beats off the same comic engine.
instructions: 1) State your premise's base reality (the normal world) in one sentence. 2) Identify the single unusual thing (the 'game') - the first funny deviation. 3) Write the first beat that demonstrates it. 4) For each new beat ask: 'If this unusual thing is true, what ELSE is true?' and write a fresh, more specific example of the same game - never repeat the same beat the same way. 5) Go general-to-specific and heighten 3+ times. 6) Stop before the logic breaks. 7) Audit: every beat must serve the one game, not introduce a second.
setup: a premise with one clear comic deviation
origin: UCB Comedy Improvisation/Sketch 201 (game of the scene)
variations: Improv version: play it live, each player adds one 'what else is true' beat in turn.

name: Find-the-Game Script Diagnosis
description: Take any draft scene or bit and locate its game by hunting for the first genuinely funny moment, then rebuild the piece around repeating and heightening only that.
instructions: 1) Read your draft scene/bit/story. 2) Mark the first line or moment that's actually funny - that's almost certainly your game. 3) Cross out funny attempts that aren't that game (competing jokes dilute it). 4) Rewrite so every subsequent beat is a variation that repeats-and-heightens the marked game. 5) Add variation: never deliver the game the same way twice. 6) End on the most specific/extreme version.
origin: UCB Sketch 201 (Drew Tarvin class notes)
variations: Do it on a produced sketch/sitcom scene to train your eye before using your own work.

name: Ninety-Nine Jokes
description: Group joke-volume game: players take turns at a mic filling a fixed walk-into-a-bar template with an audience-suggested subject, training fast punchline generation and 'selling' weak lines.
instructions: 1) Get a suggestion from the group (an occupation, object, animal). 2) Players queue and take turns at a 'mic' (real or imaginary). 3) Each delivers: 'Ninety-nine [subject]s walk into a bar. The bartender says, "I can't serve ninety-nine [subject]s," and the [subject]s say, "[your punchline]."' 4) Punchlines should play on the subject's traits, puns, or behavior. 5) Keep a brisk pace; balance quality with quantity. 6) When the well runs dry, get a new suggestion. 7) Optional: award points for the biggest laughs to crown a winner.
origin: Improv long-form/short-form game library (ImprovDr)
variations: Solo version: write 20 different punchlines for one subject against the clock.

name: Good-Bad-Worst Advice Panel
description: Three-person panel game where audience questions are answered by one good adviser, one bad adviser, and one giving catastrophically terrible advice - trains escalation and commitment to a bad idea.
instructions: 1) Seat three players as an 'expert panel' with a host. 2) Host assigns roles: Player 1 gives genuinely good advice, Player 2 gives bad advice, Player 3 gives the absolute worst advice imaginable. 3) Host takes a real question from the audience ('How do I ask for a raise?'). 4) Each adviser answers in turn, in role; the worst adviser commits fully to the disastrous take. 5) Take several questions; rotate roles. 6) Debrief which 'worst' answers were funniest and why (usually confident + specific + logical-but-wrong).
origin: ComedySportz / improv advice-panel format
variations: Solo writing version: answer 5 advice-column questions three ways (good/bad/worst) on paper.

name: World's Worst
description: Fast line game: given a scenario, players step forward one at a time to embody the world's worst person at it in a single line or image, training one-line premise generation.
instructions: 1) Players stand along a back line. 2) A caller names a category: 'World's worst person to sit next to on a plane / world's worst surgeon / world's worst wedding toast.' 3) When an idea strikes, a player steps to center, delivers one line or strikes one image embodying the worst version, then steps back. 4) Keep it rapid - short, punchy, no scenes. 5) Refresh with a new category when energy dips. 6) Solo: write 15 'world's worst' lines for one category on paper.
setup: a group (works solo on paper too)
origin: Improv short-form canon (ImprovDr, Thiagi Group)
variations: Written one-liner version; or 'World's Best but secretly awful'.

name: Heckler Repeat-Back Drill
description: Rehearse the repeat-back move - asking a heckler to say it again - to buy thinking time, expose weak heckles, and set up a comeback under pressure.
instructions: 1) Have a partner throw you scripted and improvised heckles. 2) Practice the loop: (a) calmly ask them to repeat it; (b) listen; (c) read the room's reaction; (d) deliver your response; (e) optionally repeat their line back a third time, which often deflates it. 3) Build a personal bank of 'shared' all-purpose put-downs graded mild/medium/strong, plus bespoke ones referencing your own look/age/background. 4) Drill matching response intensity to heckle type. 5) Run 10 exchanges; debrief which comebacks landed.
origin: Stand-up craft (Chris Head; Geoff Whiting)
variations: Write a bespoke put-down for every line of a transcribed real heckle exchange.

name: Comparison Two-Column Mining
description: Pick two subjects, list every association for each in parallel columns, then mine the overlaps and surprising contrasts for comparison jokes.
instructions: 1) Choose two subjects - one your topic, one to compare it to (can be unrelated). 2) Make two columns. 3) Under each, freely list associated words, traits, clichés, and images - don't force connections yet. 4) Scan for overlapping or clashing keywords between columns. 5) Build jokes asserting the similarity in the setup and exposing a surprising difference (or vice versa) in the punch. 6) Keep the 3 sharpest links.
origin: Comedians on the Loose joke-writing techniques
variations: Force the second subject to be random (open a dictionary, point).

name: Statistic Afterthought One-Liners
description: Use real or absurd statistics as setups, then add an afterthought that takes a surprising attitude or deliberately misreads the number.
instructions: 1) Collect 10 statistics (real headlines or odd survey facts like '8% of people pronounce Wi-Fi wiffy'). 2) For each, state the stat plainly as a setup. 3) Add an afterthought payoff that either (a) takes an unexpected attitude to it, or (b) wilfully misinterprets what the number means. 4) Write at least one per stat; push for 30 across a session to keep ~10. 5) Tighten: cut words, end on the funniest word.
origin: Chris Head, Lesson 11: Writing Wordplay One-liners
variations: Inspirational-quote version: use a motivational quote as setup, knock it down cynically.

name: Saying Recompletion
description: Begin a well-known saying so the audience predicts the ending, then complete it with a surprising twist - a fast, reliable misdirection one-liner form.
instructions: 1) List 10 sayings, proverbs, or cliches with predictable endings ('Behind every great man...', 'Money can't buy...'). 2) Say each normally up to the point of expectation. 3) Replace the expected ending with a surprising one; the bigger the departure (while still making sense), the bigger the laugh. 4) Write 2-3 endings per saying and keep the best. 5) Read aloud to confirm the misdirection lands on the final word.
origin: Chris Head, Lesson 11; classic 'afterthought/recompletion' gag form
variations: Saying-reversal version: take the saying literally and build a scenario around the literal meaning.

name: Idiom Beforethought (Wordplay Reverse-Build)
description: Start from a phrase or idiom that has two meanings or a homophone, treat it as the payoff, and build a setup backwards so both meanings fire at once.
instructions: 1) Google an idiom list, or collect homophones/double-meaning phrases ('it hit me', 'Chinese whispers'). 2) Pick one as your intended PAYOFF. 3) Work backwards: invent a literal scenario where the phrase's other meaning is literally true. 4) Write a setup for that scenario - but avoid using the payoff's key word in the setup (or the surprise dies). 5) Land the phrase as the final beat so both meanings collide. 6) Produce several; keep the cleanest.
origin: Chris Head, Lesson 11: Writing Wordplay One-liners
variations: Pun-payoff version: take any pun and reverse-engineer a clean setup that hides the key word.

name: Hide the Payoff Word
description: Editing drill that strengthens any joke by removing words from the setup that telegraph the punchline, using synonyms, specifics, or roundabout phrasing.
instructions: 1) Take 5 of your existing jokes. 2) Identify the key word(s) in each payoff. 3) Scan the setup: is that word (or an obvious cue to it) present? If so, the surprise is leaking. 4) Rewrite the setup to avoid the word - use a synonym, a specific detail, or a roundabout phrasing (e.g. say '12:59' instead of 'one' if the punch needs 'one'). 5) Read before/after aloud; the concealed version should land harder. 6) Add this as a permanent step in your editing checklist.
origin: Chris Head, Lesson 11; standard one-liner craft
variations: Reverse audit: deliberately leak the word, then fix it, to feel the difference.

name: Question-What-Nobody-Questions Drill
description: Observational drill: pick an everyday ritual everyone accepts and relentlessly ask why it exists, mining the arbitrary or absurd logic underneath for material.
instructions: 1) Each day pick one mundane routine or convention (tipping, the urinal gap, 'how are you' as a greeting). 2) Ask: why does this exist? Who decided this? What if I refused? 3) Write the absurd assumptions baked into it. 4) Phrase your strongest finding as a setup ('Why do we...?') and draft a punch that exposes the absurdity. 5) Keep a running 'why does this exist' list to pull from.
origin: Observational-comedy pedagogy (Seinfeld 'noticing' strategies)
variations: Contradiction-collector version: log 5 gaps between what people say and what they do.

name: It-Was-So-X-That Exaggeration Drill
description: Fixed hyperbole template that forces fresh, specific exaggerations by completing 'It was so [quality] that ___' with the most extreme believable image.
instructions: 1) Pick a topic and the quality you want to amplify (so quiet, so cheap, so boring, so cold). 2) Complete the template: 'It was so [quality] that ___' with a concrete, surprising consequence ('My apartment was so quiet I thought the flies were studying'). 3) Write 5 completions per quality; the early ones are obvious, the later ones funnier. 4) Make the consequence specific and visual, not generic. 5) Keep the best as one-liners or tags.
origin: Standard humor-writing technique (The Write Flourish; comedy-device guides)
variations: Understatement flip: describe something huge with deadpan minimization ('mild inconvenience').

name: Blind Spot Persona Builder
description: Build a stand-up persona by naming a real personal flaw, exaggerating it, and giving your stage self a 'blind spot' - they're oblivious to the very flaw the audience sees clearly.
instructions: 1) List your genuine flaws (ask close friends: am I controlling, negative, awkward, mean, vain?). 2) Pick the truest one. 3) Exaggerate it to an absurd degree. 4) Create the blind spot: on stage you do NOT see this flaw - you present as its opposite (a controlling person who insists they're easygoing). 5) Give the persona an agenda: something false it's trying to convince the audience of, and will fail to. 6) Write 3 jokes where the gap between how you see yourself and how you obviously are is the engine.
origin: Comedians on the Loose (stage-persona method); Steve Kaplan straight/wavy-line theory
variations: Attitude-list version: from a list of positive/negative qualities, friends pick 3 of each that fit you; build the persona from those.

name: Contrary Attitude Rant
description: Pick something authority or society calls bad and spend two minutes committedly arguing it's actually good - surfacing your contrarian comedic point of view.
instructions: 1) List 5 things 'everyone agrees' are bad (skipping the gym, eating alone, ghosting, being late). 2) Pick one. 3) Set 2 minutes. 4) Argue out loud, fully committed, that it's actually GOOD - with specifics and mock-conviction. 5) Record it; mine the most confidently absurd lines. 6) The strongest become opener premises that announce your persona's worldview.
origin: Stand-up persona/POV pedagogy (Stand Up Comedy Clinic; common class drill)
variations: Reverse: argue that a beloved thing (puppies, weddings, summer) is secretly terrible.

name: Song Parody Rewrite
description: Take a well-known song and rewrite its lyrics for comic effect while preserving melody, meter, and stress - training rhythm, economy, and sustained comic premise.
instructions: 1) Pick a song you know cold; rap or lyric-dense pop gives more syllables to work with. 2) Write out the original lyrics. 3) Choose a single comic concept strong enough to last the whole song (the song is about doing laundry; about your commute). 4) Replace lyrics line by line, matching syllable count and keeping word stress on the musical accents - even one extra syllable dulls the joke. 5) Front-load setups so punch words land on strong beats. 6) Sing it aloud to test scansion; fix any lines that trip. 7) Build to a strongest joke at the final chorus.
setup: a known song and its lyrics
origin: Parody-songwriting tradition (Weird Al Yankovic method)
variations: Genre-swap version: perform a serious song in a wildly wrong style; or parody a jingle/anthem.

name: New Choice
description: Improv wit game: a side-coach 'dings' a player mid-scene and they must instantly replace their last line or action with a different one, training rapid alternative generation under pressure.
instructions: 1) Two players improvise a scene from a suggestion; a third person calls 'New choice!' (or rings a bell). 2) On each call, the player must immediately swap their last line for a different one - and can be dinged repeatedly, forcing a 3rd, 4th, 5th alternative. 3) Each new choice should still make sense in the scene. 4) Keep going until the funniest option surfaces (often the later, weirder ones). 5) Debrief: notice how your first instinct is rarely your best.
setup: 3+ people (or a partner who calls dings)
origin: Short-form improv canon (Whose Line / Theatresports)
variations: Solo written version: write a line of dialogue, then 5 'new choice' replacements for it.

name: Alphabet Scene
description: Two players improvise a scene where each successive line must begin with the next letter of the alphabet, forcing inventive, often absurd phrasing under constraint.
instructions: 1) Get a scene suggestion and a starting letter. 2) Player A's first line begins with that letter (say A), Player B's next line with B, and so on through the alphabet. 3) Keep the scene coherent and advancing while obeying the letter constraint. 4) Lean into the funny contortions the constraint forces (X, Z lines especially). 5) Aim to complete the alphabet in about 90 seconds. 6) Reset with a new letter and scenario.
origin: Theatresports / Whose Line short-form game
variations: Solo writing version: write a 26-line monologue, each sentence starting with the next letter.

name: Scenes From a Hat
description: Pull comedic scene prompts from a hat and perform quick blackout-style bits for each, training rapid premise execution and finding the joke fast.
instructions: 1) Beforehand, write many funny prompts on slips ('things you can say to your dog but not your boss', 'rejected superhero powers', 'world's worst first-date openers'). 2) Put them in a hat. 3) Draw one and immediately perform or pitch the funniest short response - one line or a 10-second bit, then blackout. 4) Move fast; multiple players can jump in on the same prompt. 5) The discipline is getting to the joke in the first beat. 6) Keep the prompts that generate the most material for later writing.
origin: Whose Line Is It Anyway / short-form improv
variations: Solo: draw a prompt and write 10 one-line answers; great for list-joke and tweet material.

name: Three Perceptual Positions Act-Out
description: Greg Dean's funny-storytelling drill: tell a personal story while consciously switching between three positions - Narrator (to the audience), Self-in-scene, and other Characters - to mine humor from acting it out.
instructions: 1) Pick a true story with conflict and strong emotion (an argument, a mishap). 2) Map three positions: NARRATOR (you, talking to the audience, setting up and cracking wise), SELF (you, replayed inside the scene), CHARACTER (others/objects you portray). 3) Run it: narrate the setup, then drop into the scene and act out the back-and-forth as Self and Character, popping back to Narrator to comment. 4) Find the funniest in-scene act-outs (voices, postures, exact dialogue). 5) Record and tighten which lines play best in which position.
origin: Greg Dean, Anatomy of Funny Storytelling
variations: Conversation version: practice telling the same story at dinner, leaning harder into act-outs each time.

name: Gibberish Translation
description: One player 'speaks' an emotional nonsense language while a partner 'translates' it into surprising English; the comedy lives in the gap between tone and translation.
instructions: 1) Pair up: one Speaker, one Translator (get a topic - a speech, a how-to, a confession). 2) Speaker delivers a passionate monologue in pure gibberish - real cadence, big emotion, gestures, NOT monotone. 3) Speaker pauses in chunks; Translator 'translates' each chunk into English that matches the EMOTION but surprises with specifics. 4) Heighten: let the translation reveal increasingly absurd content under the grand delivery. 5) Swap roles. 6) Debrief which translations got the biggest laugh (usually committed delivery + unexpected specifics).
origin: Improv canon (Spolin/Johnstone lineage; ImprovDr, learnimprov)
variations: Solo: deliver a known speech in gibberish on camera, then write the funniest possible 'subtitles'.

name: Comic Throughline Map
description: Vorhaus tool for longer pieces: map a single comic premise across a beginning-middle-end so the same incongruity escalates to a climax instead of jokes wandering.
instructions: 1) State your comic premise as the gap between a comic reality and the real one ('a man who treats his cat like a coworker'). 2) Write the THROUGHLINE: where the premise starts (mild), 3-4 escalation beats where the incongruity intensifies, and the climax (most extreme expression). 3) Audit each beat: does it raise the stakes of the SAME premise, or wander to a new one? Cut wanderers. 4) Add tension-and-release: build pressure, then pop it at each beat. 5) End on the biggest, most inevitable version. 6) Apply to a bit, sketch, or story.
origin: John Vorhaus, The Comic Toolbox (comic throughline; tension and release)
variations: Rule-of-Nine pairing: generate nine premise beats expecting one to survive; map the throughline from the keeper.

name: Tension-and-Release Reps
description: Drill the build-up/pay-off rhythm: deliberately stretch the setup to build anticipation, then release it with the punch, testing different build lengths.
instructions: 1) Take a joke or short story with a clear punch. 2) Write/perform it three ways: minimal build (straight to punch), medium build (one extra tension line), long build (stack 2-3 lines that raise expectation or stakes before the punch). 3) Record all three. 4) Listen for where the release lands hardest - too little build = no payoff, too much = audience drifts. 5) Mark the optimal build length. 6) Practice the 'pop': land the release on the final, funniest word, then stop talking.
origin: John Vorhaus, The Comic Toolbox (tension and release)
variations: Story version: practice withholding the key detail to stretch tension, then release.

name: Character Physicality Walk
description: Build funny characters for act-outs by changing how you walk and hold your body part by part, letting physicality generate personality and voice.
instructions: 1) Stand neutral. 2) Change one physical lead at a time: walk toe-heel, then on inside edges of feet, then outside edges, then lead with the chest, then the chin, then the belly. 3) For each, notice the personality and voice that emerges - say a line in that body. 4) Pick the funniest 2-3 bodies and name them (the chin-leader = the smug boss). 5) Improvise a 30-second monologue in each. 6) Bank these physical characters for act-outs in your bits.
origin: Physical-comedy/acting pedagogy (theatre character-physicality drills)
variations: Animal version: walk as an animal, then humanize it 50% to find a character.

name: Just a Minute
description: Speak for 60 seconds on a surprise topic without hesitation, repetition, or deviation; rivals challenge you, and the comedy comes from the scramble to stay legal.
instructions: 1) One player gets a random topic and must talk for 60 seconds. 2) Three rules: no HESITATION (no pauses/um), no REPETITION (don't repeat a notable word), no DEVIATION (stay on topic and make sense). 3) Other players may buzz in to 'challenge' a breach; if correct, they take over the topic for the remaining time. 4) Score points for correct challenges and for speaking when time runs out. 5) Be funny while staying legal - the constraint forces playful tangents and wordplay. 6) Rotate topics and starters.
setup: topics, a timer, a buzzer or hand-raise
origin: BBC Radio 4 panel game (Ian Messiter, 1967)
variations: Solo: record yourself doing 60-second runs on random nouns; self-flag any hesitation/repetition.

name: Intentional Misinterpretation Drill
description: Practice deliberately 'misunderstanding' a phrase - taking the literal, alternate, or absurd reading - as a fast conversational comedy reflex.
instructions: 1) Collect 15 everyday lines people say ('Can you give me a hand?', 'I'm dying for coffee', 'What's the damage?'). 2) For each, write the deliberately wrong reading - literal, second-meaning, or absurd ('Give you a hand? I'm not a surgeon'). 3) Keep it playful, never hostile. 4) Drill aloud for speed: partner feeds lines, you fire the misread within 2 seconds. 5) In real conversation this week, catch one literal-reading opportunity per day. 6) Note which misreads land vs. confuse.
setup: list of common phrases; optional partner
origin: Conversational-humor/banter pedagogy; classic comedy 'misunderstanding' trope
variations: Malapropism version: deliberately swap a word for a similar-sounding wrong one.

name: Amplify and Agree
description: Comeback drill: instead of denying a tease or insult, agree with it and exaggerate it to an absurd degree, defusing the jab and getting the laugh.
instructions: 1) List 10 common jabs you might get ('you're so short', 'you're always late', 'nice pancakes'). 2) For each, agree and overshoot to absurdity ('Short? I get my clothes from the American Girl doll section'). 3) Drill aloud for speed: partner throws light jabs, you amplify-and-agree within 2 seconds. 4) Keep tone warm and self-amused, not defensive. 5) Bank your best three as all-purpose responses. 6) Field-test: next time someone teases you, try it.
origin: Witty-banter / social-skills pedagogy
variations: Pair 'roast-and-amplify': trade light jabs, each must amplify-and-agree before countering.

name: Affectionate Tease + Compliment Reps
description: Practice gentle teasing of a friend's harmless quirk immediately balanced with a genuine compliment, building playful banter that stays kind.
instructions: 1) Identify a friend's harmless quirk (over-organized, always early, loves a niche show). 2) Write a light tease that pokes the quirk ('You alphabetize your spices?'). 3) Pair it with a sincere compliment ('...honestly I admire that discipline'). 4) Aim for a 2:1 compliment-to-tease ratio overall. 5) Drill: write 10 tease+compliment pairs for people you know. 6) Deliver one per day in real life; note reactions, adjusting warmth.
origin: Conversational-humor pedagogy (banter guides)
variations: Self-tease version: tease your own quirk then reframe it as a strength.

name: Useless Superpower Questions
description: Build and deploy a bank of playful 'twist' questions (e.g. 'what's your most useless superpower?') that reliably spark funny back-and-forth in conversation.
instructions: 1) Write 10 absurd/twist questions: 'What's your most useless superpower?', 'What crime would you be surprisingly good at?', 'What's the worst possible name for a cruise ship?'. 2) For each, prepare your own funny answer first (modeling invites theirs). 3) In conversation, drop one and 'yes-and' their answer - build on it rather than topping it. 4) Track which questions consistently produce laughs and keep them in rotation. 5) Retire questions that fall flat; write fresh ones weekly.
setup: notes app for your question bank
origin: Conversational-humor/banter pedagogy
variations: Group icebreaker: everyone answers the same absurd question, vote funniest.

name: Association Speed List
description: Daily one-minute drill listing everything a random object reminds you of, building the associative speed that underpins fast, witty connections.
instructions: 1) Set a 1-minute timer. 2) Pick a random object in view (a mug, a stapler). 3) Rapid-fire write everything it reminds you of - memories, look-alikes, uses, feelings, related words ('mug = morning, pottery class, mugshot, a punch, hot chocolate'). 4) Don't judge; quantity over quality. 5) Next day, new object. 6) Weekly, scan lists for the surprising associations and turn 2-3 into comparison jokes or banter lines. The reps make connections fire faster live.
origin: Witty-banter / improv association pedagogy
variations: Pair version: partner says a word, you free-associate aloud for 20 seconds without stopping.

name: THREES Checklist Pass
description: Run each draft joke through Helitzer's six humor ingredients - Target, Hostility, Realism, Exaggeration, Emotion, Surprise - and rewrite to strengthen whichever is weakest.
instructions: 1) Take 5 draft jokes. 2) For each, rate presence of all six THREES ingredients: is there a clear TARGET? Can phrasing raise audience HOSTILITY toward it? Is the underlying REALISM/truth visible? Would EXAGGERATION sharpen it? Is there an EMOTION hook in the setup? Is the SURPRISE maximized at the end? 3) Find the missing/weak ingredient and rewrite to add it. 4) Re-rate; the strongest jokes score on all six. 5) Cut jokes that can't be made to hit at least four.
origin: Mel Helitzer & Mark Shatz, Comedy Writing Secrets (THREES formula)
variations: Diagnostic version: take a bombed joke and identify which of the six ingredients was missing.

name: Hostility Target List
description: Helitzer's material-generation drill: list everything you feel genuine hostility toward, vent freely about why, and harvest premises - because hostility plus truth is a reliable laugh engine.
instructions: 1) Free-list people, things, institutions, and situations you feel real hostility or frustration toward - no self-censoring. 2) For each, write why it frustrates you, exaggerating your emotional state to full rant. 3) Don't try to be funny; just vent honestly and specifically. 4) Review: the items with the most heat and specific grievances are your strongest premises. 5) Narrow each hot target to a single sharp premise sentence. 6) Develop the top 3 into bits using your joke-structure drills.
origin: Mel Helitzer & Mark Shatz, Comedy Writing Secrets
variations: Love version: list things you irrationally love and over-defend them.

name: Add Act-Outs with Space Work
description: Judy Carter's drill: convert a told joke into a performed one by turning the people/objects in it into act-outs, then add mimed 'space work' to make the act-out physically real.
instructions: 1) Take a joke where you currently just TELL what happened. 2) Find the moment to act out - become the person or thing in the joke (your boss, your dog, the GPS voice). 3) Replace narration with first-person dialogue in their voice. 4) Add space work: mime the objects and environment (hold the invisible phone, open the invisible fridge) so the scene is physically real. 5) Record; check the act-out lands harder than the told version. 6) Add act-outs and space work to 3 jokes.
setup: video recorder; existing jokes; room to move
origin: Judy Carter, The Comedy Bible (Act-Out, Space Work)
variations: Pair version: a friend calls out which line to act out, you must instantly perform it.

name: Topic + Attitude = Premise Worksheet
description: Carter's premise builder: combine a TOPIC with your ATTITUDE about it to write a sharp premise sentence that cuts to the chase, the springboard for jokes and act-outs.
instructions: 1) Pick a topic you're passionate about. 2) Write your honest ATTITUDE toward it in one phrase (love/hate/confused/scared). 3) Combine into a premise that cuts to the chase - not a description of what happened, but the pointed claim ('Online dating is a job interview where both people lie on the resume'). 4) Test it: does it state a clear opinion AND imply jokes? 5) Generate 3 jokes off the premise, then add an act-out. 6) Repeat for your top 3 topics.
origin: Judy Carter, The Comedy Bible (setup = topic + attitude + premise)
variations: Mind-map version: mind-map your top 3 topics first, then pull premises from the densest branches.

name: Association List + Find the Connector
description: Greg Dean warmup: build a long association list of specific details about a topic, then hunt for words with two interpretations (connectors) to seed misdirection jokes.
instructions: 1) Pick a topic. 2) Ask 'what are all the things I can think of that relate to this?' and list specific, identifiable details - aim for 30+. 3) Scan the list for any word or phrase with two possible interpretations (a connector). 4) For each connector, note the expected interpretation (the target assumption a setup would create) and an alternate one. 5) Write a setup that leans on the expected meaning, then a punch that reveals the alternate (the 2nd story). 6) Mine several connectors from one list.
origin: Greg Dean, Step by Step to Stand-Up Comedy (Joke Map / association list)
variations: Speed version: 1-minute association list, then find one connector in 60 seconds.

name: Premise Deconstruction (Monologue Mining)
description: Improv-derived premise generator: speak truthfully on a one-word prompt for 1-2 minutes, then deconstruct the recording for behaviors, characters, objects, and phrases to mine into joke premises.
instructions: 1) Pick one random word. 2) Record yourself talking honestly about it for 1-2 minutes - real memories and opinions, no jokes. 3) Play it back and flag anything that makes you smile. 4) Deconstruct it across categories: patterns of behavior (recontextualize them), emotions expressed, details to heighten with 'what if', minor characters to transplant into new contexts, objects with wordplay, locations with comic weight, standout phrases. 5) Turn the 5 richest finds into premise sentences. 6) The low pressure surfaces premises you'd never write cold.
origin: Armando / monologue-deconstruction improv (Armando Diaz), adapted solo by English Comedy Frankfurt
variations: Group Armando: one person monologues, the team improvises scenes inspired by details from it.

name: Deadpan Delivery Drill
description: Practice delivering absurd or funny lines with a completely flat affect - neutral face, monotone, no winking - so the comedy comes from the gap between content and delivery.
instructions: 1) Take 5 absurd statements or your own punchlines. 2) Record yourself delivering each with ZERO emotional emphasis: neutral face, even pitch, no smile, no build. 3) Resist 'selling' it - the deadpan wants the audience to almost miss the joke for a beat. 4) Compare to an animated take; note which lines actually get funnier dry. 5) Practice the 'no reaction' hold after the line - don't laugh at your own joke. 6) Field-test one deadpan line per day in conversation.
origin: Dry-humor/deadpan performance pedagogy (Backstage; comedy-delivery guides)
variations: Contrast version: deliver the same line deadpan vs. big-and-animated; keep whichever is funnier.

name: Fortunately / Unfortunately
description: Group story game where each person adds a sentence alternately starting 'Fortunately' or 'Unfortunately', building an escalating comic tale through constant reversals.
