instructions: 1) Sit in a circle. 2) Player 1 opens with a neutral first sentence ('Jeff woke up late for the wedding'). 3) Player 2 adds a sentence starting 'Fortunately...', Player 3 'Unfortunately...', alternating around the circle. 4) Each turn must reverse and escalate the situation logically but absurdly. 5) Keep the chain coherent; build toward a ridiculous climax. 6) Debrief the funniest reversals - they're often the most specific. 7) Solo writing version: alternate the two words down a page.
origin: Classic improv/storytelling parlour game
variations: Comedy-roast version: 'Fortunately/Unfortunately' about a (consenting) friend's day.

name: Joke Exquisite Corpse
description: Surrealist parlour game adapted to comedy: players blindly contribute setups and punchlines on folded paper, producing absurd joke mash-ups that spark fresh associations.
instructions: 1) Each player writes a joke SETUP on the top of a slip ('Why did the accountant cross the road?'), folds it to hide it, and passes left. 2) Without seeing the setup, the next player writes a PUNCHLINE under the fold and passes again. 3) After a round, unfold and read the mismatched setup/punch pairs aloud. 4) The accidental juxtapositions are the point - mine the funniest collisions. 5) Variation for material: pass premises and have the next person blindly write a tag. 6) Keep any combination that accidentally works.
origin: Surrealist Exquisite Corpse game adapted to joke writing
variations: Single-word version: build an absurd sentence word-by-word, then find the joke in it.

name: Specific Self-Deprecation Drill
description: Write self-deprecating jokes about your real minor flaws, made so vividly specific and imaginative that they read as confident and funny rather than sad.
instructions: 1) List 10 of your minor, situational foibles or one-off embarrassing moments (not deep insecurities). 2) For each, write a joke that's RIDICULOUSLY specific and imaginative - the specificity is what keeps it from sounding sad ('I'm so bad with names I introduced my own mother as "this lady"'). 3) Punch from a place of baseline confidence - you're choosing to roast yourself, not begging for reassurance. 4) Keep a 'less is more' rule: pick your best 3, not all 10. 5) Test one in a speech opener or conversation; gauge whether it lands warm.
origin: Self-deprecation/public-speaking humor pedagogy
variations: Reframe version: end each self-burn with a defiant flip that turns the flaw into a weird strength.

name: Object Transformation (Props)
description: Take an everyday object (or no object) and rapidly demonstrate it as many different things as possible through committed mime, training fast visual-gag generation.
instructions: 1) Hold a neutral object (a pen, a scarf, a chair) or mime an empty hand. 2) On a 9-second clock, transform it: show it as a sword, a toothbrush, a baby, a fishing rod - each with distinct physical use and an attitude. 3) Commit fully and treat it as the new thing; the humor is in the speed and creativity, not length. 4) Solo: do 20 transformations of one object against the clock and note the funniest. 5) Group 'Props': teams get a weird object and pitch comedic uses as quick blackout gags. 6) Mine the best transformations for visual bits.
origin: Whose Line 'Props' / Canadian Improv Games object-transformation
variations: The Gift: a partner hands you an imaginary object; you instantly define it as something specific and react.

name: Setup-Reveal-Escalation Sketch Build
description: Write a sketch from a single comic idea using a fixed structure - setup, reveal, escalation, pay-off - keeping one game and two clashing points of view.
instructions: 1) Pick ONE comic idea/game (e.g. a prudish clerk refusing to sell an embarrassing item). 2) Define two clashing POVs: one reasonable character, one unreasonable - each convinced they're right. 3) SETUP: establish who/where/what they want in 3-4 lines. 4) REVEAL: land the bizarre element in one clean hit. 5) ESCALATION: repeat and vary the same conflict, upping absurdity each beat - introduce NO new ideas. 6) PAY-OFF: end on a reversal (the reasonable character adopts the unreasonable view) or a false-dawn fail. 7) Read aloud; cut anything off-game; keep it under ~2 pages.
origin: Chris Head, How Comedy Sketches Work
variations: Constraint: write three different reveals for the same setup, then pick the strongest to escalate.

name: Press Conference / Expert Game
description: One player fields rapid questions as a secret expert or identity they don't know, inventing confident, funny answers on the fly while piecing together who they are.
instructions: 1) Send the 'guest' out of earshot. 2) The group decides the guest's secret identity or absurd expertise ('world's leading authority on breadcrumbs'). 3) Bring them back; they hold a press conference. 4) Reporters ask questions that hint at the secret without naming it. 5) The guest must answer every question in character, confidently and comically, even before they've guessed who they are. 6) Funny comes from committed, specific, confident wrong-sounding answers. 7) Game ends when the guest correctly guesses their identity. 8) Rotate.
origin: Improv short-form canon (Press Conference / Expert)
variations: Interrogation version: a 'suspect' must justify an absurd secret crime under questioning.
